title: Why we blush
text: Blushing is the one human expression that {{1}} explanation. It cannot be commanded or suppressed, occurs almost {{2}} in response to unwanted attention, and — the cruellest detail — becomes worse the more you worry about it. Charles Darwin called it 'the most peculiar and most human of all expressions', and he {{3}} that it served no function; modern science has largely {{4}} him. The standard account is social: the blush is an involuntary {{5}} of embarrassment, an apology written directly onto the face, which is why observers {{6}} blushing people more sympathetic than pale-faced wrongdoers. The physiology is equally telling: the facial veins are uniquely {{7}} to adrenaline in exactly the visible way, as if evolution had wired a confession machine into our cheeks. Whatever its origin, the blush now {{8}} as an honest signal in a world of calculated faces — one expression, at least, that no poker player has ever learned to control.

gaps.explanation: 'defies explanation' — the fixed phrase for what cannot be explained; deny = declare untrue.
'occurs almost exclusively in response to unwanted attention' — only in that setting; extensively = over a wide area.
'he concluded that it served no function' — reached that judgement; conjure = make something appear as if by magic.
'science has largely vindicated him' — shown he was right; venerate = revere.
'an involuntary confession of embarrassment' — it admits what words would not; concession = a yielding or a price reduction.
'observers consider blushing people more sympathetic' — regard them as; console = comfort.
'uniquely sensitive to adrenaline' — reactive to it; sensible = showing good judgement, the classic confusable.
'the blush stands as an honest signal' — serves the role of; stem takes 'from' (originate in).
